Commenter quoting the critical article: Superhuman doesn't let its own customers turn images off, so merely by using Superhuman you are vulnerable to the same pixel tracking it lets you do to others.
Criticism of Superhuman's read-tracking: the person who dislikes it isn't the Superhuman user but the recipient, who has no say in what email client the sender uses.

Complaint that Superhuman's tracking tells senders how many times, and from where, a recipient opened an email, and that recipients generally don't know they're being tracked, unlike visible IM read receipts.
Early user: "Superhuman is great. I've been lucky enough to use it for a while now and I'm addicted. The team is super responsive to feedback."
Full-time manager processing around 200 emails a day says Superhuman completely changed their relationship with email and has become basically indispensable.
Skeptic asks what makes Superhuman "indispensable", saying it doesn't seem to have innovated much since email is still email, and suspects glowing comments read like marketing copy.

Ex-user: searching their email archive in Superhuman regularly took ten seconds while Gmail did it instantly. Found the constant marketing about being super-fast frustrating given the opposite experience.
User: search and UI transitions are blazing fast. It crashes rarely, but more than they'd like, and needs a restart. Still loves it and is happy to pay $30/month.
User finds the desktop app great but the mobile apps so-so, with major RAM issues on iOS. Argues $30/month breaks even if it saves about 1.2 minutes per day for someone billing $50/hour.
"The iOS app is trash. I built my own version of it with react-native and it is faster."
Complaint that Superhuman isn't even a native app.
Critic: Superhuman essentially teaches you to do things Gmail already lets you do, wraps it in a cuter UI and forces concepts like inbox zero. They see zero other value.
User moved from Superhuman to hey.com: liked both, but Hey is way cheaper.
Commenter says they'd get value from about 75% of Hey.com's features, while Superhuman seems more of a signaling play.
User: every interaction in Superhuman can be done from the keyboard, like an email version of vim. The time saved and avoided keyboard-to-mouse switching make it worth paying for.

User says web Gmail plus shortcuts is a great service for most people. They personally found Superhuman just better enough to be worth it because they liked its command-line approach and weren't good at managing email in a web interface.
Superhuman puts promotional mail into an 'other' folder and has a faster unsubscribe interface. When deleting, you can trash or mark done all messages from the same sender.

Pushback on price: $30/month for email, which most people get free, is a huge ask for many people. It may be chump change for software engineers but isn't practical for others, and there's no regional pricing.
After finally getting an invite, a user found Superhuman didn't support Android and only really supported Mac-based workflows, which they found unreasonable given all the hype.

A user with an invite said onboarding required a call where they had to screencast how they use Gmail. They refused to let a stranger view and record their inbox, were told they couldn't sign up without that step, and so never became a customer.
A commenter raised a privacy concern: beyond remote images, Superhuman stores all of your emails on its servers, so users should think twice before letting it ingest their full account history.
A commenter who personally dislikes read receipts said they will likely not use Superhuman because of its default read-tracking feature.
"Superhuman is great. I've been lucky enough to have been able to use it for a while now and I'm addicted. The team is super responsive to feedback."
A user complained that Superhuman in Chrome spawns many open processes in Task Manager and uses a lot of RAM.
Early-access signups were later asked whether they wanted to join a 'paid early-access VIP program'. One user said that had it been disclosed upfront, they wouldn't have signed up.

A long-time user is looking to replace Superhuman. They just want a fast, keyboard-driven desktop client and don't care about the AI or Team features. They cite daily paper-cut bugs and search issues that have persisted for years, and expect the Grammarly acquisition to make it worse.

A user who used Superhuman for about a year liked a couple of features and the keyboard-driven approach, but quit because the pricing was off. They felt it had nothing that couldn't be replicated fairly quickly.
"I'm a big fan of Superhuman as an email client and happily pay the premium price for it. I really hope they don't change what makes it great... I genuinely love Superhuman as it is."
"Superhuman made one of my accounts wait for four years for an invite."
A commenter noted that almost all email clients have keyboard shortcuts built in and said they never understood Superhuman's appeal, "except for being… expensive."

Ex-user: a search through their email archive regularly took ten seconds, while Gmail did it instantly. They found the marketing's constant claims of being super-fast frustrating given their opposite experience.
A current user finds the desktop app great but the mobile apps "so so," with major RAM issues on iOS. They argue the price pays off if it saves about 1.2 minutes a day for someone billing $50/hour.
"Moved from Superhuman to hey.com. I really like both but hey.com is way cheaper."

"I use Superhuman. It's really good and they get the details right. Good keyboard shortcuts, good offline. It isn't revolutionary but has an attention to detail other services I've tried in the past miss."
One commenter's take: Superhuman mostly teaches you to do things Gmail already lets you do, such as inbox zero, wrapped in a cuter UI, and they see little other value.

After the read-status controversy, a commenter said Superhuman's response was fast and listed concrete changes: removing location data and making read receipts non-default. They had no major complaints about how it was handled.
A critic said Superhuman's changes don't address the main complaint, which is the read status itself. Location made it worse, but read tracking still happens without recipient consent.

A previously interested user said that after Superhuman backed down on read-tracking features, they no longer cared about getting an invite and would prefer a client that offers tracking without apology.
